Minimal Detectable Change

Source: R/mdc_test.R
mdc_test.Rd

Estimates the minimal detectable change (MDC), also called the smallest detectable or real difference, the "minimal difference" (Weir, 2005), or the repeatability coefficient: the smallest change in one subject's score between two occasions that exceeds measurement error with a given confidence. It is a scaled standard error of measurement (SEM), so it comes with a confidence interval and an optional test against a change that matters, and is returned as an object of class "htest".

Usage

mdc_test(
  x = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  measure = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  col.names = NULL,
  mdc.level = 0.95,
  sided = c("two.sided", "one.sided"),
  k_avg = 1,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  null.value = NULL,
  alternative = c("less", "greater", "two.sided"),
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A formula of the form values ~ item | id, or the result of reli_err_test() or reli_facet_test() with stat = "SEM", whose SEM is then used without refitting. Leave NULL to use measure, item and id (long data) or col.names (wide data).

data

A data frame containing the variables.

measure, item, id

Column names (character) of the measurement, the item (trial, rater, or occasion) and the subject identifier, for data in long format.

col.names

Column names (character) of the items, for data in wide format (one row per subject).

mdc.level

The confidence that a change of at least the MDC is not measurement error (default 0.95, the "MDC95"). This is not the confidence level of the interval, which is conf.level.

sided

"two.sided" (default) for a change in either direction, or "one.sided" when only a change in one stated direction (e.g. an improvement) is of interest. A one-sided MDC95 uses the same multiplier as the two-sided "MDC90".

k_avg

The number of measurements averaged at each occasion (default 1). Use it when the score used in practice is the mean of several trials: the MDC then shrinks by \(\sqrt{k_{avg}}\).

conf.level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

null.value

A change that matters, on the scale given by scale, to test against: by default (alternative = "less"), whether the MDC is below it, i.e. whether a change of that size can be distinguished from measurement error. It should come from an external anchor; see Details. The default, NULL, gives the estimate and interval without a test.

alternative

"less" (default), "greater", or "two.sided". The default tests whether the error is smaller than null.value. Used only when null.value is given; without a test the interval is two-sided.

...

Further arguments passed to reli_err_test() when x is not an existing result: scale, model, type, method, boot, boot_ci, replicates and se_method.

Value

A list of class c("reli_htest", "htest"), as for reli_err_test(), containing:

statistic, parameter, p.value

The test of the SEM (equivalently of the MDC), when a null.value was given.

conf.int

The confidence interval for the MDC.

estimate

The MDC, on the scale given by scale.

stderr

Standard errors of the MDC and of its log.

null.value

The change tested against, if any.

alternative, method, data.name

As for an htest.

percent

With scale = "log", the MDC and its interval as a percentage increase and decrease.

sem

The SEM result the MDC was computed from.

fit, data, settings, boot

As for reli_err_test(); settings also holds the MDC settings and multiplier (mdc).

Details

Estimate. A change score is the difference between two measurements, each with error SEM, so its error SD is \(\sqrt{2} \cdot SEM\), and $$MDC = \frac{z \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot SEM}{\sqrt{k_{avg}}},$$ with \(z\) the standard normal quantile for mdc.level (1.96 for a two-sided MDC95; Weir, 2005, eq. 13) and \(k_{avg}\) the number of measurements averaged to give the score at each occasion (k_avg; 1 for single measurements). The mean of \(k_{avg}\) measurements has error \(SEM / \sqrt{k_{avg}}\), so averaging shrinks the MDC by the same factor. The SEM is from reli_err_test(), with the same model, type and scale choices; the defaults give the typical error of Hopkins (2000), \(\sqrt{MS_E}\). With two trials the MDC equals the half-width of the limits of agreement of agreement_limit(), which also reports the bias between trials.

Interval and test. Because the MDC is a fixed multiple of the SEM, its interval is the SEM interval times that multiple, and the test of \(H_0: MDC = \) null.value is the SEM test of null.value divided by it (a \(\chi^2\) test for the SEM, or the bootstrap with boot = TRUE). With scale = "log" the MDC is in sympercents; percent gives the equivalent percentage increase and decrease, which differ: \(100(e^{MDC/100} - 1)\) and \(100(1 - e^{-MDC/100})\).

Differences between raters or devices. The same reasoning applies to two measurements of one subject by different items, such as two raters or two devices, rather than two occasions: the MDC is the difference between them that measurement error alone would exceed only 5% of the time (for 95%). When the raters are interchangeable (any rater's score is used as it is, and raters are thought of as drawn from a pool), use type = "agreement", so that systematic differences between raters count as error; the consistency SEM leaves them out and understates how far apart two raters can be. For two particular raters, the limits of agreement of agreement_limit() report their bias and the spread around it separately. This is the MDC, not a multiple of the standard error of prediction (SEP): the SEP concerns a change from a subject's estimated true score (Weir, 2005), and \(1.96 \cdot SEP\) does not bound the difference between two raters.

Repeat measurements. When each rater measured each subject more than once, pass an SEM from reli_facet_test(): with facet = "intra" the MDC is for two measurements by the same rater (on two occasions, with occasion), with facet = "inter" and type = "agreement" for two measurements by different raters drawn from the pool. Averaging is then set in reli_facet_test() (k_avg, m_avg, r_avg), and k_avg here must be 1.

An individual threshold, not a group one. The MDC applies to a single individual's change between two measurements. It is not a threshold for an average (group) effect. The uncertainty in a mean change shrinks with the number of subjects (its standard error is about \(\sqrt{2} \, SEM / \sqrt{n}\)), so a mean effect well below the MDC can be estimated precisely and be clearly different from zero. Judge a mean effect by its own confidence interval. An effect smaller than the MDC is small relative to one person's measurement noise; that does not make it noise itself, and it does not show that the effect is absent!

Nor should the MDC be used to count "responders". An individual's observed change mixes their true response with within-person variation from occasion to occasion, so the proportion whose change exceeds the MDC reflects measurement noise as much as real differences between people: even if every subject had exactly the same true response, some would exceed the MDC and some would not (Senn, 2004). Real differences in response are estimated from the variance of the change scores in a treated group compared with a control group, or from replicated crossover designs (Atkinson & Batterham, 2015; Senn, 2016).

The MDC and the smallest worthwhile change. The MDC describes measurement noise. It answers the question: how large an observed change must be before it can be distinguished from error? Whether a change matters is a separate question that the reliability data cannot answer. There needs to be an external anchor, such as a clinically important difference or a change that alters competitive outcomes. Give that value as null.value (with the default alternative = "less") to test whether the MDC is below it.

A "smallest worthwhile change" (SWC) computed from the same reliability data cannot serve as that anchor. With SWC = 0.2 times the between-subject SD (Hopkins, 2004), \(SWC / SEM = 0.2 / \sqrt{1 - ICC}\), a restatement of the ICC. Hopkins (2004) offers it as a default (e.g. for fitness tests in team sports) when no relationship to a real outcome is available, and it should be treated as such a fallback.

Hopkins's (2004) SWC for solo athletes, 0.3 times the CV, is an external anchor, but only with the right CV: the within-athlete variability of top athletes' performance from one competition to the next, not the test's own typical error. Simulations (Hopkins, Hawley & Burke, 1999) showed that an enhancement of 0.3 of that CV gives a top athlete about one extra win in 10 events. That CV can be estimated with reli_err_test() (scale = "log") from repeated competition results, with competitions as items, and 0.3 times it given here as null.value. Applied to the test's own CV instead, the rule is circular: \(SWC / MDC = 0.3 / (1.96 \sqrt{2}) \approx 0.11\) for every test. The anchor also rests on the one-in-10 convention and on elite fields of evenly matched athletes; for athletes further back in the field, Hopkins works out the worthwhile enhancement case by case.

References

Atkinson, G., & Batterham, A. M. (2015). True and false interindividual differences in the physiological response to an intervention. Experimental Physiology, 100(6), 577-588. doi:10.1113/EP085070

Hopkins, W. G. (2000). Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Medicine, 30(1), 1-15. doi:10.2165/00007256-200030010-00001

Hopkins, W. G. (2004). How to interpret changes in an athletic performance test. Sportscience, 8, 1-7.

Hopkins, W. G., Hawley, J. A., & Burke, L. M. (1999). Design and analysis of research on sport performance enhancement. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 31(3), 472-485. doi:10.1097/00005768-199903000-00018

Senn, S. (2004). Individual response to treatment: is it a valid assumption? BMJ, 329(7472), 966-968. doi:10.1136/bmj.329.7472.966

Senn, S. (2016). Mastering variation: variance components and personalised medicine. Statistics in Medicine, 35(7), 966-977. doi:10.1002/sim.6739

Weir, J. P. (2005). Quantifying test-retest reliability using the intraclass correlation coefficient and the SEM. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 19(1), 231-240. doi:10.1519/15184.1

See also

reli_err_test() for the SEM; agreement_limit() for the limits of agreement; reli_htest-methods for summary(), plot() and check().

Examples

# Weir (2005) data set A: 8 subjects, 2 trials
weir <- data.frame(t1 = c(146, 148, 170, 90, 157, 156, 176, 205),
                   t2 = c(140, 152, 152, 99, 145, 153, 167, 218))
mdc_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir)
#> 
#> 	Minimal detectable change (95%, two-sided) from the standard error of
#> 	measurement (two-way, consistency)
#> 
#> data:  t1, t2
#> 
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  13.84918 42.63152
#> sample estimates:
#>      MDC 
#> 20.94635 
#> 

# Can a change of 30 units be distinguished from measurement error?
res <- mdc_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, null.value = 30)
summary(res)
#> The test is not statistically significant (X-squared(7) = 3.41, p =
#> 0.156; MDC = 20.9, 95% upper bound 37.6) at the 0.05 alpha level. The
#> null hypothesis cannot be rejected: at the desired error rate, it
#> cannot be stated that the true MDC is less than 30. The estimate is the
#> minimal detectable change (two-way, consistency), in the units of the
#> measurement, from the SEM excluding systematic differences between
#> items: the smallest change in either direction between two measurements
#> of one subject that exceeds measurement error with 95% confidence, 1.96
#> * sqrt(2) * SEM. It applies to an individual's change, not to an
#> average (group) effect, which should be judged by its own confidence
#> interval. The data had 8 subjects and 2 items (16 measurements, none
#> missing); variance components were estimated by analysis of variance.
#> The interval and chi-square test are exact under normality (chi-square
#> distribution of the error variance).

# From an existing SEM, one-sided, as a percentage (log scale)
# in the result we can access the MDC on the percentage scale (converted from sympercent)
sem <- reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, scale = "log")
res_log <- mdc_test(sem, sided = "one.sided")
res_log$percent
#>     change estimate    lower    upper
#> 1 increase 12.42008 8.047983 26.90570
#> 2 decrease 11.04792 7.448527 21.20134
